rv.q: It's a performance that never *feels* actorly – every word, every hesitation seems real and true and heartfelt.
Underpinning the project, too, is the ovation-worthy ambition of exploring what life is like now, in our brave new, sadder, post-Covid world.
Flawed, but rich and thoughtful, it's a show that welcomes the return of theatre as a space to confront ideas together.
It is ambitious, engaged on many fronts, and forward looking in a way that's rare for theatre.
Ian Rickson’s steady-hand direction can’t compensate for the fact that, though the play establishes many potentially fascinating plot strands, it soon loses momentum.
Yet despite it all, this is a becalmed evening.
Walden is an apocalyptic vision that sometimes comes close to turning into a well-intentioned lecture.
Walden is a big, ambitious play that ends up collapsing somewhat under the weight of its own ideas.
The intensity of the mood is gripping; it makes you want to listen and argue.

While Berryman’s play is set in the future, when climate change has completely ravaged the Earth, it’s moments like these that make the story feel eerily prescient, albeit with its fair share of plot holes and loose ends.

So Walden, which of course includes some good speeches about Henry David Thoreau’s book, whose subtitle is Life in the Woods, as well as some other fine passages, has too many ideas, but not enough raw emotion.
If her neat conceptual balance is only intermittently successful, it’s encouraging to find a new writer happy to grapple with big ideas.
Walden might seem a fine idea on paper but in practice, it is lost in space and that makes for a very slow-moving performance.
The humourless script by New York writer Amy Berryman is static and vastly over-laden with exposition.
If the intention of this season was to remind us of the joy of theatre, then this opener is a triumph.

cn.t: Berryman's ambitious climate-crisis debut divides critics with its thought-provoking premise but sluggish execution. While some praise its timely themes and detailed production, others find it overladen with exposition and too lecture-like.
